blocks.content: Parliament may in exercise of its constituent power amend by way of addition, variation or repeal any provision of this Constitution in accordance with the procedure laid down in this article.

rows: Admission/formation of new states, official language, citizenship
Fundamental Rights, DPSP, and major structural provisions
Requires consent of half of state legislatures if federal structure is affected

items: Joint sittings under Article 108 are NOT allowed for Constitutional Amendment Bills in case of a deadlock between the two Houses.
Prior permission of the President is NOT required for introducing a Constitutional Amendment Bill in Parliament.
Amendments passed by a simple majority (e.g., creation of new states under Article 3) are not considered amendments under Article 368.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Article 368 in Part XX of the Indian Constitution deals with the constituent power of Parliament to amend the Constitution.
Parliament can amend any provision of the Constitution by way of addition, variation, or repeal in accordance with the laid-down procedure.
The Supreme Court in the Kesavananda Bharati Case (1973) established that Parliament cannot alter the 'Basic Structure' of the Constitution.
An amendment bill can be introduced only in either House of Parliament, and not in state legislatures.
The President is bound to give assent to a Constitutional Amendment Bill as per the 24th Amendment Act, 1971.
